title: Metta Sutta, Part 3: The Teachings on Loving Kindness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of recognizing and challenging our own conditioning, particularly when it comes to cultivating loving-kindness meditation. Nomon Tim Burnett suggests that we often create conditions for ourselves to feel a certain way, only to find fault with others who fail to meet those expectations. By acknowledging and letting go of our own conditioning, we can develop a more authentic and compassionate practice of metta, or unconditional loving-kindness.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Nice to see you.
I keep being sort of amazed that we have such great attendance this summer.
That's nice.
I brought some handouts.
I didn't make enough.
I keep doing that because I think nobody's going to be there.
This is funny.
I feel like I'm just parachuting in to give a talk.
Who's this guy?
Last week I was with my family on the north end of Vancouver Island.
The towns are called Port Hardy and Port McNeil and Telegraph Cove.
It was beautiful and sort of tragic, like all places are.
Beautiful because hardly any people are there and there are very few sources of pollution.
The waters and the marine ecosystem are in pretty good shape.
We went out on the whale watch boat and saw, in short order, 25 or so orcas and a couple of humpback whales and rafts and rafts of sea birds, just everywhere.
It was wonderful.
Actually, we were on the boat for my dad's birthday, which was one of the purposes of the trip.
It was for him to get through his first birthday since he was widowed.
And that seemed to go fine for him.
But one of the things that felt tragic was that, it turns out, human beings have contrived to turn the entire island into an enormous tree farm.
You just drive down these highways and there's nothing but trees.
And their signs will say, "Oh, these trees have been here since 1982.
Isn't that great?"
There's a whole forest.
And so then I got home.
I mean, there are still a few trees, and green and beautiful.
There aren't even paved roads in a lot of places.
You're driving down these gravel roads and these endless tree farms.
There are even company towns run by the logging company.
And I guess the B.C. government's plan for forest management was just basically, "Go for it.
Here you go."
Anyway, we went through one of these company towns to go to a beautiful park, Cape Scott Park, the very northernmost tip of the island.
We didn't get to the very tip, but we went on this beautiful hike.
It's this gorgeous old-growth forest that somehow got set aside.
So then I get back and I'm thinking about the Metta Sutta, because I want to continue talking about it.
And I'm thinking one of the amazing things about the Metta Sutta and this idea of loving-kindness is its unconditionality.
This idea that we could wish well of other beings without any conditions, whether they make tree farms or not.
And ironically, what's on the schedule this week is to do some construction at home, making a little playhouse for my son and some other stuff.
So I drive to Home Depot to buy those trees, to support those tree farms.
As I pull into the parking lot (so that's ironic already), I'm thinking, how can I work with this feeling of complicity and guilt?
And yet also, what a beautiful thing, to be able to use these trees to make something.
Then when I pulled into the parking lot, there was a whole section of it with all this cross-hatching and markings.
So it must be the disabled handicap place.
And there's a truck there, must have been driven by a guy, this big truck with a big trailer, parked crosswise in a triple part, with the trailer that way all through that whole area.
And I'm thinking, God, what a schmuck.
Can you believe this?
It's taking up all the handicapped spaces, obviously not a handicapped person.
Why would he have this big truck and trailer?
So I'm noticing these conditions, right?
And I get out and I look, and it's the trailer parking.
That's what all that cross-hatching is about.
That's what you're supposed to do there.
The mind, right, creates all these conditions, and as soon as we create them, we find somebody, maybe ourself, who is failing to meet those conditions and is therefore contemptible.
And the next thing you know, you find out that your conditions are completely false.
Makes you wonder about all your conclusions, right?
We're just a raft of conclusions as we go about.
So I thought I just really want to highlight this idea of unconditionality.
And maybe one of the ways to practice with unconditionality is to notice just how powerful, unbelievable and incessant our condition creation is.
So the Buddha is trying to help us out with a little text, an unconditional love for others.

Not only did the early Buddhists keep these texts alive orally for some hundreds of years before they were written down, they also kept track of all the comments they made about them, all the stories they told about the Buddhist teachings.
That became kind of a second layer of the canon, the canonical commentary.
And that also was written down, and probably the commentary was elaborated quite a bit, but there was already an oral tradition of commentary.
You would memorize the sutra and you would memorize Ashwagosa's commentary on that sutra.
And then you would be able to recite that to your fellow monks and nuns.
So here's a story from the commentaries, which are mostly not translated into English in an organized way.
There's just too much material, I guess.
I don't know why.
The suttas and sutras themselves are pretty well translated, most of them several times, and we have good translations mostly in English for the early Buddhist sutras, including the Metta Sutta.
But not so much the commentaries.

Where you run into those is by reading contemporary commentaries on the text, where that person has Pali or has the Buddhist language and has rooted around through the commentaries to find something interesting.
Red Pine is great this way.
Someone was just talking to me about Red Pine.
He will take a short text like the Heart Sutra and then go through volumes and volumes and volumes of commentary and translate selections of that.
So if you don't know that translator, Bill Porter is really his name, but Red Pine is his pen name.
He does this.
So, the commentaries.
I feel like I've used up too much time making a comment about the commentary.
*On one occasion, the Blessed One was living at Savatthi.
When the taking up of residence of the rains was near at hand,* so the practice period was about to start.
This commentary is written as if it's a sutra too, which is funny.
*On that occasion, many bhikkhus from various countries were desirous of taking up residence for the rains*
after taking a meditation subject in the Buddha's presence approached the Blessed One.* So it's like the introduction for the practice period.
They're getting their meditation assignment.
*The Buddha expounded meditation subjects suitable for the 84,000 shades of temperament.* So there's a lot of different ways to practice: 84,000 ways.
*And there he had expounded meditation subjects suitable for the 84,000 shades of temperament in the following way.
For those of lustful temperament, he showed [unclear: "lonesomeness"] at the meditation subject.* If you're really lustful, he teaches that whatever it is you're desiring, you look carefully.
It's actually full of pus and falling apart.
It's really disgusting.
That was the way they worked with the body.
That's bad for our body image stuff to practice that way, so we don't do that.
But that's how they practiced.
They're just giving some examples of the 84,000 things.
The first was lustfulness, which requires a practice of contemplation of how loathsome things are.
*And as a subject of the 11 kinds, he showed loathsomeness as a meditation subject of the 11 kinds, as with consciousness and without consciousness.
For those of a hating temperament, the fourfold meditation subject beginning with loving kindness.*
*For those of a [unclear: "diluted"] temperament, he offered the meditation subject consisting in mindfulness of death.* You don't have much time, buddy.
*For those of a speculative thinking temperament, he offered mindfulness of breathing.
For those of a faithful temperament, the subjects consisted of recollections of the enlightened ones.
And for those of intelligent temperament, the definitions of the four elements.* So, lots of practices.
And the Buddha can, like, [unclear: "seams on your head"], too, to tell which kind you are.

*So then, a party of 500 bhikkhus had learned each their meditation subject in the Blessed One's presence and set off in search of a suitable resting place with a village as an alms resort,* looking for a place to practice for the [unclear: "range retreat"].
So they weren't all going to do it there where the Buddha was.
They got their instructions and they go off to find a good place to practice.
By a village, we can get some food.
*These bhikkhus went to an outland country, and they came inside of a mountain forming a part of the Himalaya range.*
*And its surface glittered like blue quartz crystal, and it was embellished with a cool, dense, shady green forest grove and a stretch of ground strewn with sand resembling a net or a silver sheet.
And it was furnished with a clean spring of grateful, cool water.* Yeah, it sounds like a hiking retreat.
*When the bhikkhus had spent one night there and the dawn was drawing near, they attended to the needs of the physical frame and went for alms into the town not far distant.*
*The town was connected with a thousand clans and constructed as a community residence, and the people there had faith and confidence in the Dharma.
The local villagers were overjoyed.
They fed the [unclear: "mugs"] and begged them to spend the retreat there.* Now please stay.

*Since it is hard in the outlands to get a sight of those gone forth into homelessness,* monks, *they were happy and joyful when they saw the bhikkhus, and they fed them and begged them to stay for the three months of residence of the rains.*
*And they had 500 work rooms built.* Busy townspeople, make your huts right away.
*And furnished with the necessities.
Beds, chairs, pots for drinking and washing, and so on.* So that sounds pretty good.
*On the following day, the bhikkhus went into another town for alms, and thereto the people served them in that manner and begged them to stay for the rains.
The bhikkhus consented [unclear: "subject"].*
I'm not sure what that meant, but anyway.
*So then they re-entered the wood, and they decided to keep up their energy day and night so they would practice constantly by having a woodblock struck for the watches.
And abiding in reasoned attention, they went to the roots of the trees and sat down.* So I guess they're saying they're going to have a sesshin.
They went off, "Okay, thank you, villagers.
We actually have to go meditate really intensively for a while."
But they're kind of going to two different towns.
Yeah, that's kind of confusing.
I don't know what the other towns are about.
You're getting a good reception, you're going to keep going.
I don't know.
So anyway, now they're hunkered down in the woods.
They're not just hanging out in the 500 huts.
They went to the woods.
So now here's the problem.
Finally we have a problem with this funny story.
The stories are pretty funny.
*The tree deities were discouraged by the bhikkhus' [unclear: "courage"].
They were discouraged.
They came down from their own mansions and wandered back and forth with their children.
Just as when a block of houses is commandeered from villagers by kings or royal ministers, and the human inhabitants of the houses have had to evacuate and go live somewhere else at a distance.*
So the tree spirits feel displaced, in other words.
Funny way of saying that.
*And the tree spirits thought thus, these bhikkhus who enter upon a period of residence for the rains will be here for three months.
And we cannot live with that.* So in other words, the bhikkhus just showed up and didn't pay attention to the spirits and sort of took over the woods.
I should probably truncate a little more.
This is really a strange [unclear: "rain"].

*So in the night, when it was the bhikkhus' time to give effect to the monk's true ideal,* so in the middle of the night, the turning point of the night, *the spirits created [unclear: "terraforming forms"] to chase the bhikkhus away.* They created forms of spirit.
*And standing in front of each monk, they made dreadful noises.
When the bhikkhus saw these forms and heard these noises, their hearts quelled, they grew pale and jaundiced.
They could no longer unify their attention.*
*When they were harassed again and again by this fear, their attention [unclear: "un-unified"], they forgot their mindfulness.* Which is really bad.
Forgot their mindfulness.
*And as soon as they had forgotten their mindfulness, the deities saw their opening and harassed them with bad smells.
In their brains, their brains seemed to smother in the stench with feelings of repression in their heads.*
And not just for another story, your head feels like some guy took a strap around it.
It's a whole description of a strong guy behind you tightening the strap.
Okay.
However, the bhikkhus did not mention their hauntings to each other.
Next morning, they didn't talk about it.
It's all my fault.
Yeah, right.
That's what we would be like, right?
It's a silent retreat.
You're going to [unclear: "inter-break"] the silence, admitting what a terrible meditator you are.
These nasty smells and horrible thoughts all night.
Sound, ghostly sounds.
So they haven't figured out it's the spirits.

Then one day, when all had assembled at the time for waiting on the senior elder of the community, so they're having a dharma talk, the senior asked them, "Friends, when you first entered into this wood, the color of your skin was pure and bright.
But now you are lean and pale and jaundiced.
What does not suit you here?"
So somehow one of the monks is actually noticing what's going on.
And one of the bhikkhus said, "Venerable sir, at night, I admit, I saw and heard a dreadful object and I smelt a dreadful smell.
And so my mind was not concentrated."
And then they all told one after the other of the same thing that had happened to them.
Five hundred of them, one by one.
The senior elder said, "Friends, two kinds of entry upon residence for the rains have been described by the Blessed One.
And this resting place does not suit us.
Let's go back to the Blessed One and ask for another place."
So there's something wrong with this place.
It looked nice, but now we know.
The others agreed.
And so they went and put all their resting places in order, took their bowls and their robes, and without telling any of the villagers, slunk off, for they had no attachments among these clans.
You can relate to these guys, all right?
You can go into town and say, "Well, we can't hack it.
Sorry."
You just leave.
And so they returned eventually to the Blessed One in Savanti.
When the Blessed One saw them, he said, "Bhikkhus, a training rule has been made known by me, saying that no one should be going wandering during the rains.
Why are you wandering here?"
They told the Blessed One what had happened.
The Blessed One averted to the whole of the Jambudvipa, talked to the whole world.
No, he looked around the whole world.
So he looked around the whole world with his celestial sight.
And he saw not so much as even a place for a four-legged chair that would suit these monks as a resting place.
Look around the whole world.
There's nowhere that's going to make these guys happy.
And then he told them, "Bhikkhus, there is no other resting place that will suit you.
It's only by living there where you were that you might reach the exhaustion of the taints.
So go back and occupy that same resting place.
But if you want to be free from fear of spirits, then learn this safeguard, for this will be both a safeguard and a meditation subject for you."
And then he uttered the Metta Sutta.
Hearing this, and then hearing the returning monks reciting the sutra when they arrived, the tree deities welcomed the bhikkhus to the forest and now kept them safe in support of their practice.
So I thought you'd enjoy knowing where this comes from, supposedly.
And also I think it's relevant to us because we've had some powerful experiences, each of us, with spirits, if you want to call them that, at this place that we go for our week-long retreats.
And so it occurred to us to do some kind of ceremony.
We've tried different things, but the ceremony we're doing now is centered around the Metta Sutta for this reason: the Metta Sutta is a statement of intention and itself a practice.
A practice of love, of recognition of all kinds of beings, including beings that can't be seen.
Did you notice that in there?
It says very specifically that you should devote your love and attention to beings that you cannot see.

So the first part of the sutra, which we talked about some time, two weeks ago, was about the virtues that we should, on one hand, have in order to practice this effectively, and on the other hand, are virtues that we could develop through the practice of it.
And we talked a little bit about these two different glosses in the Buddhist tradition.
On the one hand, practice is a tool to fix, to improve us, because we're a little flawed.
And so we're not so virtuous.
We could use some work and this will help.
And on the other hand, we're already complete.
We actually are okay.
It's our own funny little mind that is always seeking trouble that convinces us that we're not okay.
So the trick here is not to take up a technique to fix ourselves, because that just exacerbates the problem, just reinforces the idea that we're broken.
So we have both glosses and we have two different translations.
So I don't know if any of you are so close to bringing that copy of that, I think, printing out twelve more.
So let's just spend a few minutes digging into the next verse of the sutra.
We might need to share this a little bit.
Before we do, actually, we're passing these out.
Did anyone take me up on the email?
Oh, here's a few more, exactly one more.
Did anyone take me up on the suggestion, or maybe you want to do it, but did anyone remember to do it?
The idea to consider one of the eleven or fifteen virtues that are mentioned in the sutra, in the beginning of the sutra, and study how that is for you?
Did anyone actually think of that?
Awesome.
Can we [unclear: "ask out what"]?
**Participant:** Yeah, I picked, just to try to be content with things as they are.
I think that's how I answered it.
That's a good practice, because the natural impulse is to wish things were a little different.
But that was helpful, to just take a look at what actually is, and try to be okay with it instead of complaining about it internally or wishing it was different or something like that.
And that's something you work on anyway, I know, but did this help to bring it into the foreground?
Yeah, just to pay a little more attention to it, just to try to.
It helps, because usually it doesn't do any good at all to add, "I don't like this, this is different."
I can just eliminate that, and even if it's something unpleasant, it's not as bad.
So that was a good practice.
I think I'll keep that.
Yeah, it's a lifetime thing, yeah.
Yeah, content with what is.
Which can mean just don't complain about what it is.
Yeah, right, yeah, non-complaining.
Wonderful.
Anyone else take up the study of virtues?
Yeah, did you?
Yeah, I chose not being so busy.
Oh yeah?
Which is ironic because I have pretty much nothing going on.

Although I'm actually in a short class now, it's a week-long class, but it went with my experience since I moved here anyways, because for the last two and a half years I've been working my way through school.
So working like 30 hours a week and then going to school and never sleeping in, always having something to do and just always having to be on top of stuff.
And then since I moved up here at the [unclear: "beginning of your life"], living in savings, it's been really, like, I thought it was just going to be awesome and relaxing, like a vacation.
And it totally has been, but there's been this part of me that's panicked at having nothing to do.
And so really just being with that, and just getting up in the morning where I don't have to pack my day with things, I can just relax, or just eat breakfast and then sit and enjoy the morning.
I don't have to fill my time and stuff.
So turning towards that impulse to, yeah, yeah, yeah.
It was just a little panicky for us.
Yeah, thank you.
Ian, did you want to share anything?
I have to.
They're easy to instruct.
Oh yeah, yeah.
There were more words.
Are you easy to instruct?
No.
Well, maybe.
Me neither.
But I found that I just started a new job, and you make a lot of mistakes when you're trying to do something that you maybe have no business doing.

And if you just [unclear: "relapse that you have"] and look like you have no idea what you're doing, you don't want to be there, because in Western society you don't get raises, you don't get recognized if you really [unclear: "argued as an idiot"].
So you're trying to, well, no, I did this because this was my thought process.
And that really is just a mess.
Just keep your mouth shut.
Say yes and do it right.
You'll be recognized eventually.
Don't fight it up front.
And so I really tried to work with that and failed a lot and succeeded sometimes.
But yeah, that really worked quite well.
That's really great.
So are you saying the thing you're trying not to do is being really successful and smart in the way you make mistakes, and bragging about your mistakes?

No, if, for instance, there's an error in workmanship and he comes back and says, you signed on this and this is really wrong, you need to do it this way, I have the strong compulsion to say, well, this was my thinking.
It wasn't my thinking, right, mostly.
Whereas it's best just to, he's a busy guy.
Everybody's busy.
Just, kind of like a [unclear: "mean manufacturer"], you don't spend time blaming.
You just fix it.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
That's very central in Zen training.
I know you too.
I can just say, thank you.
Yeah, yeah.
It was highlighted by coworkers.
I actually made a resolve to undertake the easy-to-instruct thing.
And then I noticed, I think the very next day or the day after, how incredibly combative this guy was with the boss man.
And I was like, oh crap.
Not easy to instruct.
I really need to not be like that.
That is what I was doing.
Hopefully I wasn't doing it nearly that bad.
I really need to do it a lot, a lot less.
That was really interesting.
I was just lined up like that.
Thank you.
That's really good.
Yeah, we don't hear that.
Be easy to instruct.
Yeah, it's a good virtue.
Yeah, not in the usual Western list.
So the first section, verses one and two, was pretty much about these virtues to be cultivated or to already have.
And this also works within the frame of Buddhism having three legs to the stool.
One of the sets of three, anyway.
First is virtue, the second is concentration, and the third is wisdom.
So: virtue, concentration and wisdom.

Now, according to the traditional way of looking at it, we're entering into concentration, which is what you actually do, what you actually understand, what emerges from your virtuous quality and your virtuous practice.
So we have:
*Let one do nothing that is mean, let the wise reprove.*
So those are the actions that will result.
And then we have this central assertion, probably the most famous line in all of early Buddhism:
*May all beings be happy.
May they be joyous and live in safety.*
[unclear: "Tansaravikus"] more literal translation:
*Do not do the slightest thing that the wise would later censure.
And think happy and secure.
May all beings be happy at heart.*
So let's play with some Pali here.
You actually need to have this, and maybe share with a friend if you don't have one.
So look at the Pali, the second section of verse three, which starts with:
*Sukhino, Sukhino va kemino,*
onto sabe satta, bhavantu [unclear: "saki tata"], something like that.
This phrase has two versions of the word for happiness: the very first word and the very last word.
And you can actually see it in there.
The word for happiness as a noun is suka.
It's a Pali, like Romance languages, says conjugation and stuff.
So suka means happiness.
Sukhino is one version of happiness, and [unclear: "suki tata"], tata, is another version of happiness.
So there's happiness at the beginning and at the ending.
The commentaries apparently say that the first version, sukhino, means physical well-being, so it actually feels well in the body.
And the last one means happiness more like an emotion.
But then right away with happiness we get into all kinds of glossing and trouble.
Like happiness like ha ha ha?
Or what kind of happiness?
And there's another word, piti, that gets translated as joy.
I think we tend to like the word joy.
It feels sort of more solid to us than happiness.
But anyway, it's some version of happiness as an emotion.
And then the middle part is interesting.
The word, the k-h word, ke-mi-no, ke-mi-no means physically safe.
Physically safe, [unclear: "shikir"], so free, safe from danger.
So happy and physically safe.
And hantu is an imperative form of to be.
So: may it be so.
Va is some kind of connector, I forget.
So: happy and physically safe, may this be so.
Sabah, sabah, s-a-b-b-e, is all, just a normal word for all.
And satah, s-a-t-t-a, is being.
So all beings.
And bhavantu is related to bhavanah, which is like coming into existence, which is the word used for meditation.
So putting this all together we have something like: happy, physically safe, may this be so.
All beings, bringing this forth, happy.
May all beings be happy.
May they enjoy and live in safety.
When people do metta practices, where you work with phrases, we did that on the first night of looking at the Metta Sutta, and I think I got it on the website, maybe.
I hope so.
I will if I have it.
People come up with all kinds of phrases, but they're all rooted in this phrase.
This is the only place in the actual canon where it talks about may all beings be happy, and this phrase gets repeated in different sutras.
I like to say something around may all beings be well and safe, free from danger and happy.
But you can try different phrases.
Safety is interesting.
There's a lot of elements to it, right?
There's physical safety, emotional safety, all kinds of safety.
Does that mean walls around you, that kind of safety?
What kind of safety would this be?
I think it's interesting to contemplate what would be a healthy kind of safety, something we can practice with, something that will benefit us.
And maybe there are different kinds of safety for different kinds of situations.
Maybe sometimes you should totally retreat.
Maybe another kind of safety is to see that it's possible to be okay in a place that's more dangerous.
I don't know.
It seems like it's a wish for others.
Feel safe.
Feel safe.
**Participant:** When people feel safe in that sort of sense, they are able to just sort of be themselves.
So you're really allowing, it sounds like you're really sort of allowing others to be as they are without trying to impose a happiness.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Right, right, right.
That's a nice point, yeah.
**Participant:** That our wish for happiness somehow allows for that.
As they are and the way they feel.
Allows for safety.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, good.
Any other comments?
That's a good comment.
John and Georgia.
**Participant:** If you feel safe, you can wish others well.
If you don't feel safe, that would take most of their energy and attention and it's hard to be compassionate and thoughtful about others.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Right.
What's interesting is that the traditional meditation kind of points this at different groups of beings in different directions, including at yourself.
What's funny about us, and Bob just accidentally modeled what we all do, is that it says all beings, so that means everybody else but me.
I'm not included.
That's funny, isn't it?
We do that so automatically.
All beings, that's you guys.
You're talking about life.
You deserve that.
You're free from danger.
You're free from harm.
So really kind of specific.
Yeah, real.
**Participant:** My thought about safety was it actually has less to do with the individual than everyone around.
Maybe we co-create a safe.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Very interwoven.
Great.
Now let's do just a little bit more.
What's your watch say?
Three minutes.
Three minutes, huh.
Okay, we won't do any more.
But what goes on from there, we'll look at this more carefully next time, whatever that is.
It goes on to really dig into what do we mean by all beings.
This is actually pretty important.
We tend to see this as just sort of a nice list: living, weak, strong, high, visible and invisible, as you mentioned before.

But I think the way it was intended is actually meditation instructions: to spend some amount of time practicing metta for weak beings, including yourself, and sometimes practicing metta for strong beings, including yourself.
Really kind of take each group, to be very thorough going about it.
It's not just sort of like a literary flourish.
By all means, we really mean all beings.
Everybody welcome.
I suppose we actually kind of see it as a process that we can go through.
To be continued.
So maybe the assignment is, well, you could keep working with virtues.
And I have at least one copy of that virtue sheet.
I can email you the list if you want.
Or we can copy it downstairs.
Or, and or, watch conditionality.
Watch conditionality.
It comes up constantly, at least for me.
Maybe not for you.

I don't think I would have liked him if he didn't help me.
And the cashier was pretty efficient with her scanner, so I liked her.

Maybe once in a while we could catch ourselves just coming into contact with another being and just being like, wonderful.
Another human being.

verbatim.text: Good evening everybody. Nice to see you. I keep being sort of amazed that we have such great attendance this summer. That's nice. I brought some handouts. I didn't make enough. I keep doing that because nobody's going to be there. This is funny. I feel like I'm just parachuting in to give a talk. Who's this guy? Last week I was with my family on the north end of Vancouver Island. The town's called Port Hardy and Port McNeil and Telegraph Cove. And it was beautiful and sort of tragic like all places are. Beautiful because hardly any people are there and there are very few sources of pollution. The waters and the marine ecosystem is in pretty good shape.
